Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading Arunima Sinha's Journey to the Summit

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.166): paired discussion on adventure sports and qualities of a mountaineer.

time_bands.activity: Open the chapter at the pre-reading page (p.166) and display the adventure-sport icons. Ask pairs to identify each activity and share with the class which they find most exciting and why — a quick paired exchange to warm up thinking about risk and courage.

Invite pairs to call out qualities they associate with mountaineers; build a class word-web on the board, using student suggestions. Accept adventurous vocabulary and correct any muddled terms before moving on.

Read the full informational text (p.166–169) aloud, teacher-led with students following in their books. Pause at key moments — Arunima's accident, her vow in hospital, her summit day — to ask brief confirmation questions and keep the class anchored to the sequence of events.

Open the "Let us discuss" statements (p.169). Choose two statements — Arunima as a beacon of hope, and Bachendri Pal's guidance — and invite students to explain each in their own words in a full class discussion. Correct any factual mix-ups before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The text moves quickly from the 2011 train attack to the 2013 summit; students may conflate the timeline. During the read-aloud, write the key years — 2011, eighteen months of training, 21 May 2013 — on the board to keep the sequence clear. The pre-reading discussion about adventure-sport qualities is preparation for understanding why the text foregrounds resilience and mental fortitude as its central themes.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on the Text and Listening to Opinion Speakers

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.170): extract questions on Bachendri Pal's words and Arunima's summit day.
Let us listen (p.173): match five speakers' opinions on adventure sports to eight statements.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.170): write answers to the two extended questions on Arunima as a beacon of hope and the appropriateness of her autobiography's title.

time_bands.activity: Work through the extract questions from "Let us think and reflect" (p.170) — the fill-in on Bachendri Pal's words, the inference question about Arunima's feelings, the phrase that signals exhaustion, and the MCQ on her overwhelming sense of achievement. Use a mix of cold-call and paired responses to sustain pace; confirm or correct after each item.

Introduce the listening task (p.173): explain that students will hear five speakers give opinions on adventure sports and must match each to one of eight statements (three are extra). Read the eight statements aloud and clarify any unfamiliar vocabulary before the transcript begins.
Read the transcript aloud (p.177) at a natural pace — once straight through, then a second time with brief pauses between speakers. Students note their matches on paper as they listen.

Class verification: call each matched pair aloud and ask students to justify their choice with a phrase from what they heard. Confirm the five correct matches and identify the three unused statements together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the biography of Arunima Sinha, students bring context about risk, training and resilience directly into the listening task. The three extra statements in the matching exercise are designed to test careful listening rather than guesswork — encourage students to rule out options by evidence, not elimination. The two extended reflection questions (autobiography title and beacon of hope) are set for written homework so class time is used for live discussion and listening.

periods.activity_title: Role-Play on Physical Education and Vocabulary in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.173): group role-play — student, parent, PE teacher, sports camp organiser discuss Physical Education.
Let us learn (p.171): match underlined phrases from the text with their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Distribute the four roles — school student, parent, Physical Education teacher, sports camp organiser — to groups of four. Display the prompts from "Let us speak" (p.173) on the board and give groups a moment to read their assigned role card and the vocabulary support provided.

Groups conduct the structured role-play, each member speaking from their role's perspective: arguing for or against Physical Education in school, citing safety, value or organising experience. Circulate to prompt hesitant speakers and note language errors for whole-class feedback.

Brief whole-class debrief — invite one representative from each role to share the strongest point their group made. Give targeted feedback on turn-taking, formal register and any recurring grammar errors noticed during the role-play.

Move to "Let us learn" (p.171). Read each underlined phrase from the text — exhausting days, heartfelt attempts, life-altering event, mental fortitude, beacon of hope — and ask students to predict the meaning from context before revealing the matching definition. Confirm the correct pairing for all five phrases together.

periods.teacher_notes: The role-play draws directly on the chapter's themes of sport, risk and resilience; students who played the parent or student roles often produce the most engaged argument because those perspectives are personally familiar. For the vocabulary matching, steer students away from dictionary-checking and instead ask which word in the phrase gives the biggest clue — this keeps the focus on contextual prediction rather than rote recall. The word-form table (parts of speech) is a richer task reserved for the dedicated vocabulary unit.

periods.activity_title: Articles and Word-Form Patterns in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.171): complete word-form table — noun, adjective, verb, adverb for five words.
Let us learn (p.172): fill in articles (a/an/the/x) in the adventure-trip passage and correct article errors in six sentences.

time_bands.activity: Display the word-form table from "Let us learn" (p.171) on the board with the gaps visible. Work through the five base words — determination, relief, inspire, resistance, success — one at a time, eliciting each part of speech from the class before filling in the table. Draw attention to patterns such as the -tion → -tional and -ance → -ant transformations.

Introduce articles (p.172): explain the distinction between indefinite (a/an) and definite (the) articles and the rule for choosing between a and an based on the initial sound of the following word. Work through the adventure-trip passage together, having students call out each article choice and explain their reasoning before it is confirmed.

Students correct the six article-error sentences (p.172) individually, then compare with a partner. Review each sentence as a class, identifying the type of error — a/an confusion, incorrect use of the definite article, missing article — and linking each correction back to the rule discussed.

periods.teacher_notes: The word-form table is the more demanding of the two tasks; if the class is slow on the first two words, reduce board time and move to student-pair work earlier. The most persistent article error at this stage is using 'a' before vowel-initial words — sentences (i) and (ii) in the correction exercise directly target this, so sequence those two first during review. The phrase-matching from the vocabulary work in the previous unit provides a readiness base for the word-form patterns here, as several shared roots (determine, resist) appeared in that exercise.
materials: Blackboard or display for the word-form table

periods.activity_title: Writing a Formal Letter and Planning an Adventure Sports Booklet

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.174–175): identify formal letter components, then draft a letter to the Principal for an excursion.
Let us explore (p.175): research and plan a table of five adventure sports in India.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.175): prepare an information booklet with fact sheets of five Indian mountaineers.

time_bands.activity: Open the sample formal letter on p.174 (Sreelakshmi's request to join the Adventure Club). Students read it and label each component — sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, introduction, statement of request, expression of interest, complimentary close, signature line — on their own copy, then compare labels with a partner.

Guide students to draft a formal letter to the Principal requesting a hill-station excursion for Grade 7 (p.175). Work through the structure step by step — address block, subject line, opening paragraph, request paragraph with reasons, closing — pausing after each section for students to write before the next is modelled. Students complete the full draft within the unit, then exchange with a partner for a quick peer check on format and tone.

Introduce the adventure-sports research table from "Let us explore" (p.175) — snow skiing, trekking, camping, river rafting, scuba diving — and the four columns: Name, Area, Preferred Time of Year, Equipment Required. Students begin filling in what they already know from the chapter and their general knowledge; the teacher circulates and prompts. Explain the mountaineer fact-sheet project (p.175) as an extended home task, clarifying the six fields each fact sheet needs.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently omit the subject line or write an informal salutation in formal letters; during the peer-check phase, ask partners to look specifically for those two components. The adventure-sports table is designed to be begun in class and enriched through independent research; what students complete here functions as a planning scaffold, not a finished product. The mountaineer fact-sheet project, set for independent work, asks students to apply the same kind of biographical reading they encountered in Arunima Sinha's story to five other Indian mountaineers.

items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes what Arunima Sinha decided to do while recovering in hospital after losing her leg?

options.label: A
options.text: Climb Mount Everest using a prosthetic leg.

options.label: B
options.text: Return to professional volleyball as soon as she recovered.

options.label: C
options.text: Train under Bachendri Pal at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering.

options.label: D
options.text: Write an autobiography about her accident.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses Arunima's pre-accident identity as a volleyball player with her post-accident resolve.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates the later outcome — her autobiography — with the vow she made in hospital.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student recognises Bachendri Pal's role but mistakes the sequence, placing mentorship before the vow.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to an informational biography, identifying key events and making inferences about character and theme using informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Arunima Sinha's train accident, vow, training, Bachendri Pal's mentorship, summit day, resilience themes.
items.item_stem: Bachendri Pal told Arunima, "You have conquered the Everest within you." What does this remark reveal about what Bachendri Pal considered the greater achievement — Arunima's physical climb or her inner transformation? Support your answer with evidence from the text.

expected_elements: Bachendri Pal considers the inner transformation the greater achievement.
Arunima overcame devastating trauma and self-doubt, not just a mountain.
Evidence: her vow in hospital, eighteen months of training despite disability.
Physical summit validates, but inner resolve preceded and enabled it.

items.source_lo: Student listens to multiple speakers expressing varied opinions and matches each speaker's viewpoint to the correct descriptive statement using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five speakers on adventure sports: safety concerns, thrill, supervision, school camps, traditional sports preference.
items.item_stem: Listen to the five speakers and decide whether each statement below is true or false. Write True or False next to each statement.

options.text: Speaker (ii) believes adventure sports are worthwhile only when a trainer is present.
Speaker (iii) says equipment checks are the responsibility of participants, not organisers.
Speaker (iv) promotes a wide range of high-risk adventure activities for students.
Speaker (v) prefers traditional sports such as track and field or swimming over adventure sports.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Speaker (ii) says it is worth trying "of course, with a trainer."
2. False — Speaker (iii) states the organising team ensures all equipment is regularly checked and maintained.
3. True — Speaker (v) explicitly names track and field or swimming as safer, more fulfilling alternatives.
4. False — Speaker (iv) says the school sticks to basic sports that are safe and manageable for students.

items.source_context: Five speakers on adventure sports: safety concerns, thrill, supervision, school camps, traditional sports preference.
items.item_stem: Speakers (i) and (v) both express reservations about adventure sports, yet their concerns are different. After listening to both speakers, write two to three sentences explaining how their concerns differ and what this tells you about the different perspectives people bring to the same topic.

expected_elements: Speaker (i) focuses on physical safety risks, especially for children.
Speaker (v) questions the value of risk itself, preferring fitness-based sports.
Speaker (i) is a concerned parent; Speaker (v) offers a philosophical objection.
Same conclusion, different reasoning — personal vs. values-based concern.

expected_elements: Acknowledges the parent's safety concern before responding.
Offers a reasoned opinion on balancing safety with physical activity.
Uses formal register appropriate to a teacher speaking to a parent.

items.item_stem:
A classmate has drafted the opening of a formal letter to the Principal but has placed the components in the wrong order and left out the subject line. Arrange the five components listed below into the correct order for a formal letter and add a suitable subject line.

Components to arrange:
(i) Salutation: Dear Principal,
(ii) Sender's address and date
(iii) Introduction paragraph
(iv) Receiver's address
(v) [Missing subject line — write one]

expected_elements: Correct order: sender's address and date → receiver's address → subject line → salutation → introduction.
Subject line is concise, formal and relevant to a school excursion request.
Uses formal register throughout.
All five components correctly identified and placed.

items.item_stem: Arunima Sinha's story shows how a single determined goal can transform a person's life. Imagine you are a Grade 7 student who has been deeply inspired by reading about Arunima. Write a complete formal letter to your school Principal, requesting permission for the class to participate in a one-day trekking excursion to a nearby hill. In your letter, explain why you believe the experience would be valuable for your class, referring to the qualities of resilience and teamwork.

expected_elements: All formal letter components present and correctly ordered.
Request clearly stated with reasons linked to resilience and teamwork.
Formal, polite tone maintained throughout the letter.
Closing includes complimentary close and signature line.

items.item_stem:
The passage below is about Arunima Sinha's training. Fill in each blank with the correct article — a, an, the — or write X if no article is needed.

Arunima Sinha is (1) _______ extraordinary athlete who showed (2) _______ world what determination can achieve. After (3) _______ accident that changed her life, she enrolled at (4) _______ Nehru Institute of Mountaineering in Uttarkashi. She was (5) _______ first Indian female amputee to climb (6) _______ Everest. Her story is (7) _______ inspiring example of (8) _______ human resilience.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. an  2. the  3. an  4. the  5. the  6. X (Mount Everest as a proper name needs no article here, though 'the' is also acceptable in many standard usages — accept 'the' or X)  7. an  8. X

items.item_stem: Arunima Sinha completed all Seven Summits by 2019. Choose any ONE of the Seven Summits other than Mount Everest and prepare a short fact file about it. Your fact file should include: the mountain's name and continent, its approximate height, the main challenge it presents to climbers, and one well-known mountaineer who has climbed it. Write your fact file in continuous prose of about 80–100 words.

expected_elements: Correct mountain name, continent and approximate height given.
A specific climbing challenge identified with brief explanation.
Name of one real, verifiable mountaineer who has climbed it.
Written in continuous, coherent prose of appropriate length.
